title: Marginal Tax Rates
summary: SHELVES → MARGINAL RATE → EFFECTIVE RATE → DECIDE
subtitle: You get offered more money, and a voice in your head says you might end up with less. You won’t.

blocks.text: You get offered more money. A promotion, a new job, a bonus.
And somewhere in the back of your mind, a voice says: wait, won’t this push me into a higher bracket? Won’t I actually end up with less? No. You won’t.

That fear has a name — it’s a misunderstanding of marginal tax rates — and it talks people out of raises, promotions, and side income every single year. This module exists to put it to rest, permanently.

sections.title: Picture shelves, not a single price tag

blocks.text: Forget the word bracket for a second. Picture shelves instead.
Your income gets stacked onto shelves, starting from the bottom. Each shelf has its own tax rate. The bottom shelf has the lowest rate. Each shelf above it costs a little more.
Here’s the part that matters most: your tax rate for a shelf only applies to the income sitting on that shelf. Not your whole income. Just that slice.

So when someone says “I’m in the 20.5% bracket,” they don’t mean 20.5% of everything they earn. They mean their top dollars — the ones sitting on that particular shelf — are taxed at that rate. Every dollar below it is still taxed at the lower rates of the shelves underneath.
Here’s what the shelves actually look like this year, federally.

blocks.text: Your province stacks its own shelves on top of these, at its own rates. That’s a separate calculation, and it’s why take-home pay looks different across provinces even at the same salary. We’ll leave the province-by-province detail for another module — for now, the shelf idea is what matters.

items.title: “If I earn $60,000, all of it gets taxed at 20.5% because that’s my bracket.”
items.text: Only about $1,500 of it does — the sliver sitting above $58,523. The other $58,523 is still taxed at 14%, the same as someone earning exactly that amount. Your bracket describes your last dollar, never your whole income.

blocks.text: Numbers convince better than explanations. Here’s someone earning $70,000 in 2026, federal tax only.

items.title: First $58,523, taxed at 14%. That’s $8,193.22.
Remaining $11,477, taxed at 20.5%. That’s $2,352.79.
Total federal tax: $10,546.01, before any credits.

blocks.text: Notice what didn’t happen. The whole $70,000 was not taxed at 20.5%. Only the top slice was. That’s the entire idea, in one example.
CREDIT PULSE SPOTLIGHT: MARGINAL RATE VS. EFFECTIVE RATE, THE TWO NUMBERS PEOPLE MIX UP

In that example, this person’s marginal rate is 20.5%. That’s the rate on their next dollar earned — the rate that matters for decisions like taking on overtime or a side gig. But their effective rate — total tax divided by total income — works out to about 15%. That’s the rate that actually describes how much of their whole paycheque went to tax. Both numbers are real. They just answer different questions. Marginal rate answers “what happens if I earn one more dollar?” Effective rate answers “overall, what share of my income did I actually pay?” Mixing them up is where the raise-anxiety myth comes from in the first place.

sections.title: Where this actually changes a decision

blocks.text: Understanding your marginal rate isn’t just trivia. It’s the number behind several real financial choices.

RRSP contributions. An RRSP contribution reduces your taxable income at your marginal rate — the rate on your top shelf, not your average rate. Someone earning enough to sit on the 29% shelf gets a bigger tax saving per dollar contributed than someone sitting on the 14% shelf. This is why RRSP contributions are often more valuable in your highest-earning years.

A raise or a bonus. Once you know only your top slice moves to a new rate, the anxiety mostly disappears. A raise that pushes a small sliver of your income onto a higher shelf still leaves you with more money overall. Always.

A side gig or freelance income. Extra income stacks on top of what you already earn. If your day job already fills your lower shelves, side income often lands on a higher shelf right away. Worth knowing before you spend it, so a tax bill doesn’t surprise you the following spring.

items.title: “Everyone should max out their RRSP as early as possible to save on tax.”
items.text: The tax saving is bigger in years you sit on a higher shelf. Someone in a lower-earning year, like a first job or a parental leave, may get more value contributing later, once their income — and their marginal rate — has climbed. Timing the contribution to your shelf can matter as much as the amount.

sections.title: Before you turn down extra income out of tax fear

items.title: I know which shelf my current income mostly sits on.
I understand that only new income above my current shelf moves to a higher rate.
I know my marginal rate is not the same as my effective rate.
I haven’t confused a raise with a pay cut — a raise always leaves you with more, never less.
I’ve checked whether my province adds its own shelves on top, since the full picture includes both.

blocks.text: Renata almost said no
paragraphs: Renata was offered a promotion that would push her salary from $55,000 to $62,000. Good news, on paper.
Her uncle, over dinner, told her to think carefully — he’d heard that a raise like that could bump her into a higher bracket and she might actually take home less. He meant well. He was also wrong.

Renata almost turned the promotion down. Instead, she asked a coworker who’d taken a similar jump the year before. The coworker walked her through the shelf idea in about two minutes, on a napkin, at lunch.

Only the $3,477 above $58,523 would move to the 20.5% shelf. Everything below kept its 14% rate. Renata took the promotion. Her paycheque grew, exactly as it should have — just not by quite as much as $7,000 flat, which is a very different thing from taking home less.

blocks.text: Tax brackets work like shelves. Only the income sitting on a given shelf is taxed at that shelf’s rate — everything below keeps its lower rate. Your marginal rate is the rate on your next dollar. Your effective rate is your overall average. A raise never leaves you with less money, even if a slice of it lands on a higher shelf.

items.title: Find your own income on the federal shelf table above and note which shelf your top dollar sits on.
If you’ve been offered a raise, bonus or side income and hesitated because of tax, redo the math using the shelf method before deciding.
If you contribute to an RRSP, think about whether this year’s shelf, or a future higher one, makes the contribution worth more.

blocks.text: Worksheet: know your own shelves

items.title: Marginal tax rate
items.text: The rate on your next dollar of income. Describes only your top shelf.

items.title: Effective tax rate
items.text: Your total tax divided by your total income. Your real overall average.

items.title: Tax bracket
items.text: A range of income taxed at one rate. Higher brackets never apply retroactively to income below them.

items.title: Taxable income
items.text: Your income after deductions, like RRSP contributions, are subtracted. What the shelves actually apply to.

blocks.text: Educational only, not tax advice. Figures shown are 2026 rates. Confirm your own province and year before relying on any number here.
